Hubs sell the connections that make sense

November 11, 2026 · By the Tailwinds team

A focus city with 147 routes was carrying one connecting passenger a week. Three things were wrong with how hubs sold and counted connections. They are fixed in every game, saved ones included.

  • The wrong markets were on sale. Every pair of routes at a hub is a possible connection, and a hub works through a shortlist of them each week. The shortlist was ranked by how many people travel between the two cities and nothing else. The busiest pairs among a big hub’s destinations are neighbours of each other, such as Tokyo and Osaka, so a New York hub spent its whole list offering trips like those by way of New York. Nobody took them, and the connections New York is on the way for were never offered.
  • On the way, or not sold. A hub now sells a connection only when the trip over the hub is no more than one and a half times the nonstop distance, the rule rival airlines’ connections already followed. Connections that use a partner airline’s flight follow it too. What is left is ranked by how many people travel and how little the stop costs them.
  • Bigger hubs sell more. The shortlist was 150 markets whether a hub had 20 routes or 1,500. Every route into a hub now also brings its own two best connections, so no route is left without connecting passengers because bigger cities filled the list.
  • The hub card counts passengers who boarded. It used to show everyone who chose your connection, including the ones there was no seat for. On a full network that could be several times what you carried. The card, the airport page and the Statistics chart now show the passengers you flew, and the card says when many more wanted to connect than found seats.

What changes in a saved game. Revenue barely moves for most airlines, because full flights were already the limit. The connecting figure on your hub card will change the most: it falls where flights are full and rises where the old shortlist was selling nothing.

New games seat connections differently. Until now nonstop passengers always boarded first and connections took the seats left over, one flight at a time. In every game started from today:

  • Both flights or neither. A connection is carried only when there is a seat on each of its flights, and the best fares board first.
  • A full flight can give a seat to a connection worth more. When a connecting fare is worth more than the local passengers it would displace, it takes the seat. A hub holds up to 10% of each flight this way at a Focus City, 15% at a Hub, 18% at a Major Hub and 22% at an International Gateway.
  • No route loses by it. The route that gives up the seat is paid what its local passenger would have paid, and the rest of the fare is shared between the two flights. Route Detail shows how many local passengers gave up seats.

On a test airline with a full 60-route Major Hub this was worth about 3% more revenue and 12% more profit. Saved games keep the seating they started with. More in the hub strategy guide. Thanks to Matthijs on Discord for the report.
